activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A heritage language is one spoken at home or in the family that differs from the main language of the wider community, and heritage speakers may speak it without reading it.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:42, right after dinner. Paisley had sent a photo of a birthday card covered in looping handwriting no one could read. "My grandma sent this," the message said. "She writes in Romanian. I can talk to her on the phone for an hour but I have zero idea what this says. None."

Maeva stared at the photo, then at her own reflection in the dark window. That was exactly her. She could chatter with her grandmother in Creole about school, recipes, and the neighbor's suspicious cat, but the luminous gold card on her dresser, from her own birthday last month, was still a mystery. Her grandmother had watched her open it, and Maeva had smiled and hugged her and never admitted the truth. Now Paisley's message glowed on the screen, and the truth felt heavier than it had on her birthday.

"Wait, you speak it but you can't read it?" Drake typed. "How is that even possible?"

Maeva's thumbs hovered. She thought she knew the answer, but she wanted to test it first, because a guess in a group chat stays there forever. She typed: "Question for everybody. Does anyone's family speak a different language at home than the one we use at school?" The replies came fast. Drake's mom spoke Tagalog. A kid in Ms. Otieno's class, according to Paisley, spoke Marshallese with her grandfather. Then Ms. Otieno herself appeared in the chat, since it was her classroom channel. "Heritage language," she wrote, four words, and Maeva read the phrase twice.

There it was. The pattern. A language spoken at home, in the family, that was different from the main language outside, and you could speak it every single day without ever learning its letters. Nobody had taught Paisley to read Romanian, and nobody had taught Maeva to read Creole, because school and books and street signs had all sustained only English. It wasn't lazy or strange. It was a rule, and the rule had a name, and half their class apparently lived inside it.

Then came the message that made her stop breathing for a second. Paisley: "My grandma is calling me tonight. She's going to ask what the card said." The chat went quiet. Maeva could hear her own grandmother humming in the kitchen, could smell the plantains frying, could feel the birthday card's stiff paper in her memory. She had been planning to keep pretending forever. She changed her mind in the space of one deep breath.

She typed slowly. "Tell her the truth. I'm going to tell mine tonight that I can't read her card, and I'm going to ask her to teach me. Want to learn together?" The typing bubble appeared, disappeared, appeared again. Finally Paisley answered with a single line, and Maeva read it out loud to the kitchen.

"Saturday. Bring the cards."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In formal chess, the touch-move rule says a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it, if that piece has a legal move.
story:
"Sorry, but in chess that matters," Mr. Hernández said, tapping the knight Kayla had just set back down on its square. "Touch a piece on purpose, you move it, if it has a legal move. That's called the touch-move rule."

Kayla stared at the knight. She had picked it up only to look at the horse's carved mane, and now it had to march into danger, where Deanna's bishop waited like a trap. "But we never said that rule," she protested. "We're just playing in your kitchen."

"Formal chess uses it," Deanna said, chewing the end of her braid.

Kayla moved the knight anyway. Deanna's bishop took it two turns later, and the loss felt significant, like a whole door slamming shut on her attack. She slumped until her chair creaked.

Across the table, Adeline, who had been watching from the counter with a mug of cocoa, came and sat down. "You look how I felt last week when Deanna flipped the board," she said. Kayla laughed, a small one, because she could picture it exactly. That bit of empathy loosened something in her shoulders. Instead of giving up, she decided to test an idea: if the problem wasn't the rule but not knowing the rules, she could fix that.

"Okay," Kayla said. "New game. But first let's name the problem. The problem is that some of us know tournament rules and some of us don't."

"So let's agree on one rule," Deanna said. "Say 'adjusting' before you straighten a piece. Then touch-move doesn't bite you."

"And to practice," Adeline said, "we could simulate a tournament round, complete with a clock and everything."

Mr. Hernández slid the timers out of a drawer and set the pieces back on their squares, all thirty-two of them, the pawns clicking down the rank one by one.

Kayla reached toward her queen, stopped, and said, "Adjusting."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Results from a large sample are generally more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in larger groups.
story:
Michael needed one more fact for his poster about why the town should build a rooftop garden at the library, and the library's big room was quiet enough to hear the heaters ticking under the windows. He had three surveys on his clipboard, all from his friend Gael, who had asked people whether they would eat vegetables grown on a library roof. Gael had asked his brother, his cousin, and the kid next door, and all three had said no. "Nobody wants it," Gael had said at lunch, tearing his sandwich in half. "Three out of three. Give up."

Michael spread the three surveys next to a fat binder Mr. Sokolov had left on the table, a report from a city that had tried the same thing. In that city, a survey of two hundred people had been taken, and most of them had said yes, they would eat the vegetables. Michael read the page twice. Three people said no, two hundred said mostly yes, and the numbers would not sit together in his head.

Alana dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of books about agriculture, which she had promised to find for the poster's section on how gardens work. "You look like you bit a lemon," she said.

"Three people said nobody eats rooftop vegetables," Michael said. "But two hundred people mostly said yes. Which survey do I put on the poster?"

Alana tapped the binder. "The big one. Results from a large sample are more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in bigger groups." She said it the way she said math formulas, fast and certain, then went back to her books.

Michael thought about that while he sharpened his pencil. Gael's brother hated all vegetables. His cousin hated them too. Maybe the kid next door did as well. Three people who all happened to hate vegetables was possible the way flipping three heads in a row was possible. Two hundred people could not all happen to be vegetable-haters by accident; the odd ones canceled each other out. He wrote "large sample, more reliable" on a sticky note and pressed it onto the poster sketch, right under a drawing of tomato plants in proportional boxes, one square foot each.

Mr. Sokolov came by with a cart of returns and paused at the table. "Rooftop garden?"

"Gael says nobody wants it," Michael said. "But he only asked three people."

Mr. Sokolov smiled and slid the agriculture books closer to Alana. "So recruit more," he said, and rolled the cart on toward the front desk.

Michael turned to a fresh page and started writing names: his whole class, the chess club, the line at the farmers market. Then he drew a bar for the class survey, wide and empty, waiting to be filled in.

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: A contour line on a topographic map joins points that are all at the same height above sea level.
story:
Evelyn spread the topographic map across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with mugs so it would lie flat. Grandpa's hike was on Saturday, and his knee was bad on steep ground, so she had promised to find him a route up Miller Hill that would take the gentlest way. The trouble was that the map showed no photographs, no colors of grass, nothing that portrayed the hill as her eyes would see it. There were only thin brown lines, wiggly as spilled noodles, looping around one another.

Keaton leaned over her shoulder, chewing the last of his toast. "It looks like a fingerprint," he said. "How can a fingerprint tell you which side of a hill is steep?"

"That's what I have to figure out before Saturday," Evelyn said. She read the small printing beside one of the lines. Every line had a number beside it, and the numbers climbed as the lines shrank toward the middle of the hill, 200, 220, 240. She put her finger on a line marked 220 and traced it, slow and careful, the way it curved out to the east, bulged south, and swung back around to close itself into a ring. It was like drawing the equator around a globe.

"So this whole line," she said slowly, "every single point on it, is the same height above sea level. Two hundred and twenty, all the way around." She looked at Keaton. "That means the line is like the edge of a bathtub ring. If you stood anywhere along it, your feet would be at exactly that height."

She grabbed a pencil and tested her idea. On the west side of the hill, the 220 line and the 240 line lay almost on top of each other, squeezed so tight she could barely slide her pencil between them. On the east side, the same two lines drifted far apart, with wide white paper between them. If each line was a level you climbed to, then the west side climbed from 220 to 240 in almost no distance at all, while the east side took a long, lazy stroll to gain the same height. The east slope was the equivalent of a ramp; the west was more like a wall. "The steep part is where the lines crowd together," she said. "The gentle part is where they spread out."

She called Grandpa in from the porch and traced the route with her finger, up the wide-spaced eastern lines, then along a single 260 line like a shelf halfway to the top. He tapped the trail she had drawn and grinned at her.

"Saturday," he said, "you're carrying the map."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final.
story:
The crowd on the TV roared as the players jogged onto the field, and Luca squeezed between his dad and his friend Andie on the couch, balancing a bowl of popcorn on his knees. Rain hammered the window so hard it sounded like applause, and under the oak's wet canopy in the yard, their neighbour Mr. Cohen's umbrella had blown inside out again. It was the kind of turbulent weather that made Luca glad to be inside with the final about to start.

"Beautiful game," Mr. Cohen said from the armchair. "You know who won the very first World Cup? Brazil, of course. Pelé everything."

Luca frowned. He was almost sure that was wrong, but he couldn't say why, which bothered him like a splinter he couldn't reach. "Are you sure? Brazil feels like a World Cup country, but that's not the same as being first, is it?"

"Argentina," said Luca's dad, without looking away from the screen. "Definitely Argentina."

"That doesn't work either," Luca said slowly. "If Argentina had won the first one, somebody would have mentioned it by now." Both of them couldn't be right, and maybe neither was. He slid off the couch and went to the hallway where the family kept the big encyclopaedia with the torn spine, because Dad refused to look things up on his phone during a match.

Andie followed him. "What are you going to do, read the whole S section?"

"S for soccer isn't how books work," Luca said, flipping to W. His finger ran down the page until he found it, and he read the sentence twice to be sure. Then he carried the heavy book back to the living room, held it open, and cleared his throat like a referee with a whistle.

"The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final." He looked up. "So you were both wrong, and Dad, you were wrong in the funniest way possible. Argentina lost to Uruguay. Four to two."

Mr. Cohen laughed so hard he nearly knocked over his tea, and Dad covered his face with a throw pillow. "Four to two," Dad's muffled voice said. "Demolished."

"Beaten, not demolished," Luca said, grinning. On the screen, the whistle blew and the match began.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
Ryan stood on his grandfather's porch holding a plate of samosas that were supposed to circulate through the crowd, but he kept eating them himself, so the plate was not circulating very well. Below the porch, the Vaisakhi procession rolled down the street like a slow orange tsunami, drums booming, flags whipping, and his grandfather singing along off-key on purpose just to make Ryan laugh.

Ryan's friend Zachary had come along for the food, which Zachary described as "a chronic condition I have." He pointed at a little girl walking beside a man carrying a tall flag. "Why is today such a big deal, anyway? Is it like a birthday for the flag?"

"It's a harvest thing," Ryan said. "Farming stuff. That's why there's so much food." But as he said it, he noticed something that didn't fit. The little girl's uncle was telling her a story, and every few words the crowd around them would cheer, and Ryan caught one piece of it. "Vaisakhi is the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," the girl repeated loudly, the way kids do when they've just learned something and want the whole street to know.

So Ryan had guessed wrong, and now he wanted to test the right answer. He watched what the little girl did next. She straightened her shoulders and marched like the flag bearers did, copying them step for step. When an older woman in the crowd looked tired, the girl darted over and held out her arm for the woman to lean on, just like the men with the flags were helping a wobbling toddler over a curb.

"That's the pattern," Ryan told Zachary, finally handing him the plate. "The story isn't just a story. They heard it, and now they're all taking care of each other like it's the rule."

"Then hand me a samosa," Zachary said. "You've been violating the rule for ten minutes."

Ryan passed the plate and went down to walk beside the little girl, matching her steps.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: Credit card interest rates are usually much higher than the interest a savings account pays you.
story:
Ruby wanted the blue kayak in the window of Dunmore's Sporting Goods more than she had ever wanted anything. It cost two hundred dollars, and she had eleven dollars and a birthday coming up in five months, which felt like forever away.

She was staying at Grandpa's house for the week, and she spread the problem out on his kitchen table like a detective. "I could just put it on a credit card," she said. "Mom has one. You buy the thing now and pay later."

Grandpa slid his coffee mug aside and set down a folded brochure from the bank downtown. "Before you decide, maybe evaluate both ways of doing it. We can walk over there at lunch."

At the bank, Ruby's friend Genesis was already there with her own mother, standing by a rack of leaflets. "My mom's refinancing something mysterious," Genesis said. "Want to see the free lollipops?" Ruby held up the brochure instead. One page showed what a savings account paid you, a tiny percent added to your money over time. Another page showed what the card charged you if you didn't pay it all back, and the number was far, far bigger. She read both pages three times because the difference seemed too strange to be real.

"They pay you this little," she said slowly, "but they charge you this much? That's like a seesaw where one kid weighs as much as a truck."

Genesis leaned over her shoulder. "That's an aggressive difference," she said, whistling.

"Credit card interest rates are usually much higher than the interest a savings account pays you," the cashier said cheerfully on her way past with a box of deposit slips. "Been that way my whole career." She kept walking, and Ruby stared at the two numbers again.

"So if I put the kayak on the card and take five months to pay it off," Ruby said, "the kayak gets more expensive every month I don't finish paying. But if I save up first, the bank pays me, even a little, the whole time." She turned to Genesis. "The card way, I'm paying extra for waiting. The saving way, waiting pays me."

Genesis grinned. "Want to hear an anecdote? My cousin bought a game console on a card, took a year to pay it, and it ended up costing like one and a half consoles. He cried into his pizza."

Back at Grandpa's, Ruby taped the two numbers side by side above the desk in the guest room. She had changed her mind about the card completely. Every Saturday she would walk dogs for Ms. Morales down the street, four dollars a walk, and she had done the math on a napkin: fourteen weeks, maybe thirteen if Grandpa chipped in for her birthday. The kayak would wait in the window, and she could wait too, because waiting was now on her side.

She dropped her eleven dollars into an old peanut butter jar labeled KAYAK and set it on the windowsill where it caught the afternoon light.

"Day one," she said, and shook the jar until the coins rattled like applause.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
story:
Anas answered the door in socks, holding two pairs of sneakers, and he did not look happy about it. "Third pair this year," he said. "My mom says I'm imagining it."

Inside, Edith was sitting at the kitchen table with a notebook, and she rolled her eyes at her brother. "He says his feet grow one week and stop the next. I think he just stuffs things in his shoes." Keira, who had come over to work on their science project, set down her bag and looked at the sneakers more carefully. One pair was nearly new. The other had a hole worn at the heel of the left shoe only, which was strange, because the new pair was too small for him now even though he had bought it in October. Meanwhile, she noticed, his jeans still pooled a little over his shoes, the same jeans from September. Her phone emitted a soft chime from her bag, her mother checking in, but she ignored it. Something did not add up, and she wanted to figure it out before she lost the thread.

"Stand against the wall," she told Anas. "No, in your socks." She marked his height with a pencil, then asked to see his wrists. His sleeves still reached his knuckles. She wrote the numbers down while Edith made a face that said this was a waste of a Saturday. "Here's my idea," Keira said slowly. "Maybe your feet aren't growing weird. Maybe they're just growing first, before everything else catches up. Hands and feet first, then arms and legs, then the rest." It would explain everything: shoes that stopped fitting twice in one school year, jeans that still fit fine, even the way he'd knocked over the lamp last week, because his feet had already arrived somewhere the rest of him hadn't.

Edith flipped her notebook to a fresh page and started listing the boys in their class, the ones who had shot up over the summer and the ones who hadn't yet. "If it's a pattern, we could check," she said, and Keira saw that Edith had changed her mind entirely, because now this was data instead of a brother complaining. Anas looked almost buoyant, standing there in his socks with his too-short sneakers dangling from one hand. "So I'm not broken," he said.

"You're not broken," Keira said. "You're just arriving in pieces." She picked up her phone to text her mother, and Anas went to find the second-biggest pair of shoes in the closet, the ones his cousin in the family network had passed down, the ones that might last until June.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
story:
The film club's supply cupboard door hung open, and the club's only good speaker lay on the floor in two pieces. Victoria knelt beside it while Cara hovered at her shoulder.

"I heard it fall from the hallway," Cara said. "It just went over by itself."

Ms. Dang had prescribed strict rules for the club's equipment: carry the speaker with two hands, never set it near the shelf edge, log every use in the binder. Victoria flipped the binder open. Marina had signed it out last, at 3:40.

"That's bizarre," said Marina, coming in with her backpack still on. "I put it back exactly where it always goes. Ask Theo." She pointed at the fourth member, who was pulling off his headphones.

"Wind from the window," Theo said. "I told you it was gusty in here."

Four people, Victoria thought, and four different stories. Cara heard it fall. Marina insisted she'd placed it safely. Theo blamed the window. And the binder, which couldn't lie, said only that Marina had it last. She remembered the old sandwich she'd found in the cupboard in September, furry with blue-green fungus, and how everyone had blamed a different person for that too. She'd accused Marina then, out loud, and Marina hadn't sat with her at lunch for a week. She still wasn't sure that had been fair.

On the shelf above the broken speaker sat the club's movie stack, and Victoria pulled out a case with a samurai on the cover. The back read: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.

"Cara," she said slowly, "we're in a Rashomon situation."

"A what?"

"A movie. Four witnesses, four different stories." She turned the case over in her hands. "I think we should each write down exactly what we saw, separately, before we decide anything. Then compare."

Ms. Dang appeared in the doorway, coffee in hand, and looked at the speaker. "Well?"

"Rashomon," Victoria said, and held up the case.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Fractions can only be added directly when their denominators match, because the denominator names the size of the pieces being counted.
story:
Mr. Horváth slid the fraction tiles across the table and said the bake sale committee needed a total for the recipe, then walked away, which was his way of saying figure it out.

"The recipe calls for a half cup of oats and a third cup of sunflower seeds," Avneet read off the card. "I already did it. Half plus third. Two fifths."

Nolan looked at the tiles. He picked up a half piece and a third piece and set them side by side on the mat. They did not match. The half was fat and squat; the third was slimmer. He stacked them and the edges stuck out everywhere, like two counterfeit puzzle pieces from different puzzles, pretending to fit.

"That can't be right," he said. "Look. You can't count them together. The denominator tells you the size of the pieces, and these are different sizes. A half is one big piece. A third is a smaller piece. Putting a one and a two over a five is just, like, lying."

"It's a shortcut," Avneet said, with the confidence of someone who had not anticipated being questioned.

Paige was already hunting through the tile box. "Okay, so we need pieces that are all the same size. Then we can actually count them." She laid down sixths, one after another, like a row of dominoes. Three sixths for the half. Two sixths for the third.

Nolan counted them and wrote it down. Five sixths.

"So I get more oats and seeds than my answer said," Avneet said, squinting at the two fifths tile. "I've been shorting the bake sale this whole concept of a time."

"That sentence made no sense," Paige said.

"Neither did my math." Avneet held up the five sixths tiles to the light. "Five little pieces. That's the whole cup, then?"

"That's the whole cup," Nolan said, and swept the tiles into his hand.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment, so their expectations cannot sway the results.
story:
Piper spread the three science fair packets across the library table and glared at them as if they might confess. The library smelled like old paper and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on the shelves, and somewhere behind the front desk a printer chunked out page after page. Olive arrived first, dropping her backpack with a thud, then Cedric, who was still chewing the last of his pretzels and held out the bag as a peace offering.

"It has to be the taste test," Piper said. "People say the fancy brand of hot chocolate tastes better, but I want to know if that's actually true or just what everybody repeats." She flipped to the page she'd marked, where she'd underlined a sentence twice. "The problem is, if I hand someone the fancy cup and say try this, they'll already believe it's better before it touches their mouth."

Olive leaned over the packet, her braid slipping off her shoulder. "So don't tell them which is which. Easy."

"It's not easy, because I know which is which. I might act different. I might hand over the fancy cup like it's a prize." Piper had caught herself doing it yesterday, smiling wider over one sample when she tested her little brother in the kitchen. He'd picked the one she'd smiled about. Twice.

Cedric crushed the pretzel bag flat, thinking so hard his freckles seemed to scrunch. "Then don't let the person serving know either. Get somebody else to pour the cups, swap the labels, write the code on a card and hide it. Even you won't know who got what."

Piper sat back. "That's it. That's the real thing, I read about it last night. It's called a double-blind trial. Nobody knows, not the tasters, not the people running it." She wrote it in the margin of her notes, then crossed out her old plan and drew an arrow to the new one. "Ms. Sutherland can pour while Olive and I are in the other room. We compare cups after."

Ms. Sutherland, shelving returns two rows over, agreed before Piper had even finished asking, though she had one condition. "My amendment," she said, tapping the table. "Same cups, same temperature, same amount in each. If one's steaming and one's cold, the whole thing falls apart." Piper nodded and added it. The plan on paper finally looked coherent to her, steps in a row that actually led somewhere.

Saturday morning, in the library's meeting room with the door propped open, Ms. Sutherland filled six plain paper cups and marked them with letters only she understood. Piper resigned herself to guessing along with everyone else, which felt strange and a little thrilling, like being blindfolded at her own party. Cedric tasted cup C and grimaced; Olive sipped cup F and went back for a second sip; a second grader who wandered in chose cup B so fast he clearly wasn't thinking at all. When the tasters had all pointed to their favorites, Ms. Sutherland turned over the card.

The cheap store brand had won, four votes to two. Piper laughed out loud, then wrote it down before the ink of surprise could fade. Cedric raised his plain cup like a trophy. "See? Blind people don't lie."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: A neutron has slightly more mass than a proton, so the two are very nearly the same size in a model.
story:
Anthony spread the foam balls across his father's workbench, sorting them by color in the quiet of the garage. Mr. Yilmaz, the neighbor who taught chemistry before he retired, had lent him a box of supplies and one instruction: build a lithium atom, protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons in shells outside. Anthony had three big questions, but the first was simple. Where do the electrons go?

Leif and Iver arrived on their bikes, and Iver immediately grabbed the bag of small balls. "I call electrons," he said. "They get to orbit."

"You can't call them, they're not candy," Anthony said, but he was already staring at the two piles left over, the blue balls and the red ones. Here was the problem he hadn't expected. The red balls for protons were slightly smaller than the blue ones he'd planned to use for neutrons, and the diagram in his book showed the nucleus as a jumble of both. If he used them as they were, his model would claim that protons and neutrons were different sizes. Was that right?

He held a red ball and a blue ball side by side under the workbench lamp. The blue was maybe a hair bigger. He tried gluing a red one into a test cluster, then a blue one, then pried them apart and sat very still, listening to the furnace hum in the corner. The garage felt almost tranquil while everyone waited.

"Why the frown?" Leif asked. "Just pick one."

"I can't just pick. If neutrons were way heavier, they'd be way bigger, and I'd need giant balls for them." Anthony turned the two over in his palm again, thinking about what he'd read late last night in Mr. Yilmaz's old chemistry memoir, the chapter marked with a coffee-stained napkin. "But it said a neutron has slightly more mass than a proton. Slightly. So they're nearly the same size in a model."

Iver leaned in. "So what do we do?"

"We make them the same size," Anthony said. He dug through the box until he found more red balls, enough for both, and a marker to color the neutrons blue. He glued four same-sized balls together with the three protons, hung the nucleus from a bent coat hanger, and spun the whole thing slowly over his head.

"There," he said. "Lithium."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs.
story:
Simon had been pitching at the fence in his backyard for forty minutes, and his arm felt like a wet noodle. "Faster," said Haris, who was holding the strike zone he had drawn on cardboard. "Ms. Petrov said the coach only keeps kids who can throw hard."

From the porch, Simon's sister Ellen yelled, "You're both wasting your time. The team is boys only. It says so on the flyer in the gym."

Haris lowered the cardboard. "That contradicts what I saw at registration," he said. "There was a girl in the line. Nobody stopped her."

Ellen came down the steps, spinning a softball on her finger. "Then the flyer is ambiguous," she said. "Maybe it means the team is open, maybe not. Words on gym walls are slippery." Simon had learned long ago never to argue with Ellen when she used her vocabulary face, so instead he went inside and dug through the basket of flyers and permission slips on the counter until he found the crumpled school notice. At the bottom, in tiny print, was a sentence about federal money and a rule called Title IX. He carried it out to the porch, held it up to the light, and read it aloud: "Title IX, a law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money, and it has been applied to their sports programs."

Ellen stopped spinning the ball. "So the school can't keep me out," she said slowly, testing the idea the way she tested everything. "Not if they take that federal money. Which they do, because the notice says so."

"Tryout is Saturday at nine," Simon said. "Want to practice? Someone has to throw me something faster than a noodle."

Ellen picked up the softball, backed up ten steps, and fired. The ball hissed past Simon's ear and smacked dead center into Haris's cardboard strike zone.

"Strike one," Haris announced, holding up the mangled cardboard like a trophy.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Lydia pushed off the wall and counted her strokes to the flags, the water humming past her ears. It was the first swim practice of the season, and by the end of it her arms felt warm and loose, not tired at all. Mr. Tse, who coached at the community pool every summer, told them lane four had been a mess of leaves and drowned beetle larva that morning and that whoever swam it should be grateful to the skimmer. Lydia laughed, climbed out, and walked home without a single ache.

The next morning she still felt fine, and she told her friend Layan that the practices were easier than everyone claimed. "Wait until Thursday," Layan said, wincing as she pulled her towel over her shoulder. Lydia decided Layan was making excuses, and that if she could stay painless, the rest of the team could too. She made a plan to prove it. She would time her practice sprints on Tuesday, skip Wednesday's optional session, and sprint again Thursday. If she was still fast on Thursday, then the soreness people complained about was mostly an act.

Wednesday came and went. On Thursday morning, Lydia reached for the cereal box on the top shelf and her shoulders screamed. Going down the stairs to the pool, she had to take each step sideways. At practice she could barely lift her arms out of the water for backstroke, and Mr. Tse made her kick with a board instead. Her sprint test was ruined before it started.

She sat on the edge of the deep end afterward, legs in the water, and worked it out. Monday, practice, no pain. Tuesday, no pain. Wednesday, still nothing. Thursday, two full days after practice, she could barely move. It hadn't been an act. The pain arrived late, and it arrived worst on the second and third day, not the first. She remembered Layan saying "Wait until Thursday" like someone who knew the schedule of it, and she remembered that her mother complained about stairs exactly two days after starting her aerobics class, never the morning after.

"Your legs too?" Layan asked, dropping down beside her and pointing at Lydia's careful, sideways way of sitting.

"Two days late," Lydia said. "That's the weird part. Is there a name for that?"

"Delayed onset muscle soreness," Layan said. "My sister gets it every season. It peaks between one and three days after, she says, so day two is the worst."

That matched everything Lydia had counted out on her fingers. The soreness wasn't fake, and it wasn't random; it ran on a delay she simply hadn't known to look for. She thought of the moths that had laid eggs in the pool skimmer, how the larva had appeared days later and Mr. Tse had said the pool was resilient and would be clean again by the weekend. Everything worth knowing ran on a delay, she thought, and you had to be patient enough to catch the pattern.

Friday's practice was easy again, her arms loose and light, and when Aniya climbed out of lane four rubbing her shoulders Lydia said, "Don't worry about today. Worry about Sunday."

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: Hula kahiko, the older style of Hawaiian hula, is danced to chanting and traditional instruments such as gourd drums rather than to sung melodies.
story:
The letter from Mr. Rao was taped to Maya's dance bag when she got home: "Maya, the festival changed your slot. You'll dance hula kahiko, not hula 'auana. Come Saturday ready." She read it three times on the porch, smelling the neighbor's barbecue smoke drift over the fence, and her stomach dropped. For six weeks she had practiced a smooth, modern hula set to a sweet sung melody, swaying to the tune the way she swayed to songs on the radio. Now the words on the page had transport her somewhere she had never been.

At the community hall, Adelina was already stretching on the floor. "What's hula kahiko?" Maya asked her, dropping the letter beside her shoes. Adelina looked up. "The older style," she said. "It goes with chanting and traditional instruments, gourd drums, not sung melodies." Maya frowned at the drum sitting in the corner, wide and round, its skin pale as a gourd sliced open. She had been counting on the melody to tell her where she was in the dance. If there was no tune, what would carry her?

She tested a small idea. She asked the drummer, an older woman in a green shawl, to chant one line while Maya moved only her hands, listening for the pattern underneath. The first time, Maya rushed ahead, waiting for a rise in the music that never came. The second time, she closed her eyes and found the beat in the chant itself, the rhythm pulsing like a heartbeat, and her hands landed exactly with the last syllable. "Again," she said, breathless, and this time her feet joined in.

On Saturday the festival field smelled of fried dough and cut grass, and a wind that could carry sparks made Mr. Rao move the tiki torches well back from the stage, since nobody wanted anything flammable near the canopy. Before she went on, Zayan squeezed her shoulder. "The judges' top criterion is timing with the drum," he whispered. "You've got that now." The chant began, low and steady, the gourd drum answering it, and Maya let the rhythm rise up through her bare feet. Her hands told the story of rain on the mountain, and the crowd leaned forward as one.

When the drum stopped, the silence rang louder than applause.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones and published his method in 1852.
story:
Adam stood at the edge of the soccer field with his left arm in a bright green cast, sweating even in the shade. Two weeks ago he had fallen off the monkey bars, and the doctor had asked him to pick a color. He had chosen green because it looked like the field itself, though now he wondered if that made his arm invisible to Faris's passes.

"You can still play," Faris said, jogging over with the ball under one foot. "Ms. Ionescu says you can monitor the game and call out where the ball goes. Be our eyes."

Adam tried it. At first he just shouted whatever he saw, which helped nobody. Then he began to watch Faris instead of the ball. Faris leaned left before every right-footed shot, and he dragged his heel when he meant to cross. Adam could not see Faris deciding anything, but he could see the pattern hiding underneath the movements, like footprints in wet grass. "Faris cuts left next time!" Adam called, and Faris did, and Lilia stole the ball clean.

During the water break, Lilia tapped the cast. "Does the color mean anything?" she asked.

"It's subjective," Adam said. "Faris thinks it looks like a pickle." He flexed his fingers out of the opening at the top. "The doctor said a long time ago they didn't have casts like this at all. A Dutch army surgeon named Antonius Mathijsen invented the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones, and he published his method in 1852. Before that, my arm would have been stuck in some stiff box thing for months."

"Where'd you learn that?" Faris asked.

"The poster in the doctor's waiting room. I read it six times because the TV was broken." Adam pulled his sweat-soaked sleeve away from the cast's edge, where the green was turning dark. Faris rolled the ball to him gently, and Adam trapped it under his good foot, then knocked it back with a soft, perfect pass.

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Popcorn pops because water inside each kernel turns to steam when heated, building pressure until the hard hull bursts.
story:
Lydia had never been to a sleepover before, and she was proud of how normal she looked, sitting cross-legged on a purple sleeping bag between Gwyneth and Jethro in Ms. Sutton's living room. Ms. Sutton's house had seven sleeping bags scattered like fallen dominoes, a bowl of popcorn, and a smell of burnt butter. At midnight, Ms. Sutton brought out a fresh batch, and Jethro immediately fished out the sad little kernels at the bottom, the ones that had never popped.

"Old maids," Gwyneth said, popping a good piece into her mouth. "Every batch has some."

Lydia remembered her dad making popcorn last winter, back when she was too nervous to even ask about sleepovers. He had held up a kernel and told her the water inside each one turns to steam when it's heated, and the pressure builds up until the hard hull bursts. That was the pop. She had thought it was wild, like a tiny explosion you could eat. Now she looked at the flat, stubborn kernels in Jethro's palm and a theory clicked into place.

"I bet the duds leaked," she said. "If the hull has a crack, the steam escapes and the pressure never builds enough. That would be the fundamental difference between a popped kernel and a dud. Not luck. A broken shell." She grabbed the bowl of uncooked kernels from the kitchen and held one up. "Test time. If I split a hull on purpose and heat it, it shouldn't pop."

They isolated one cracked kernel in a small pan while Ms. Sutton pretended not to supervise. The kernel sat there, hot and mute, then toasted itself a stubborn brown. "It's like me before coffee," Jethro announced, and Gwyneth laughed so hard she knocked over a sleeping bag. Lydia grinned, spooned the little failure onto a plate, and said, "Ladies and gentlemen, the world's smallest flat tire."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
story:
The timer on Georgia's phone showed 11:42, and Mr. Kovalenko's assignment was due at midnight. She stared at the screen, where a letter to the local paper glowed back at her. "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste." She had found it online while researching for her essay, and something about it itched at her. Her assignment was to explain why one sentence could be half true and half something else entirely, but she couldn't quite grab the idea with her fingers.

Her mom called from the kitchen that dinner was getting cold, so Georgia carried her laptop to the table. "Read this," she said, pushing the screen toward her dad. He squinted at it. "Two million dollars," he said. "I remember the council meeting. That number is real. I heard it myself." Georgia chewed her noodles slowly. The cost part she could picture: records, receipts, somebody's signature. But the last three words, "is a waste," were slippery. Nobody could look those up anywhere. Her dad went back to his plate, and she went back to staring.

At 9:15, Randy texted her three question marks, and Skye sent a photo of her own half-finished essay captioned "dying." Georgia typed back and forth with them for ten minutes, arguing about whether a sentence could be both a fact and an opinion at once. "It's ambiguous," Skye wrote, "like half of it floats and half of it sits still." Georgia read that line four times. Floats and sits still. She felt something click, the way a jar lid gives up all at once.

She dragged the sentence apart in a new document. The cost, two million dollars, could be checked by anyone with the patience to look. "A waste" could not, because it was an opinion, a judgment dressed up as a statement. One sentence, both things at once. She wrote fast, her fingers slapping the keys, the kitchen clock ticking louder than it should have. When she got stuck on how to end it, she remembered the city budget her dad kept bookmarking, the one with the park money circled in red, and she typed an example of her own about how the council would budget for repairs next year. Proof, she wrote, that some words invite checking and others only invite arguing.

At 11:58 she hit submit, and her heart didn't slow down until the confirmation banner appeared. Then she scrolled back to the original letter to reread the writer's name, because one thing had been bugging her all night. The signature line read "R. Kovalenko." She grabbed her phone and typed, "Mr. K? Is that you?" Three dots appeared, then vanished, then appeared again. "Check my facts," the reply said, "but argue with my opinions anytime."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
Jade arranged six paper bowls on the counter at the back of the science classroom and glared at them as if they had insulted her family. Her project was due Friday, and her hypothesis, that people could taste the difference between name-brand chocolate puffs and the store-brand kind, kept falling apart in a humiliating way. Every time she let people see the boxes, they swore the name brand tasted richer, chocolatier, more expensive. She was starting to resent those boxes, with their shiny cartoon lion, for making everyone lie without meaning to.

"Abbas, you said the store brand was bland yesterday," she said, pulling him over by his sleeve. "Today you tasted the same cereal and called it delicious. Explain yourself."

"It was in a fancy bowl today," Abbas admitted. "The one with the little flowers. I trusted the flowers."

Gibson, who was supposed to be measuring vinegar for his own volcano, drifted over instead. "Maybe people can't help it. They see the box, their brain decides the answer before their tongue even clocks in."

Jade stared at the counter. That was it. The boxes were the problem, so the boxes had to go. She stashed both bags inside Ms. Chukwu's supply cabinet, out of sight, and labeled two fresh bowls A and B with masking tape. Then she mixed up which was which, so even she was not sure. "New rule," she announced. "Nobody sees a box. Nobody knows which sample is which, so expectations can't sway their answers. Ms. Chukwu, is it okay if I call it a blind test on my poster?"

"A blind test," Ms. Chukwu repeated, nodding approvingly from her desk. "Very good."

The results after lunch were beautiful and stable: eleven testers, four correct guesses, seven wrong. Abbas got it backwards twice on the same bowl. "Your tongue has been exposed as a liar," Gibson told him solemnly.

Jade wrote the numbers in her notebook and underlined them twice. Her hypothesis was dead, which somehow felt like winning.

"Ready for test number five?" she asked, shaking a box behind her back where no one could see it.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Isabelle wanted one thing that Friday: to get the new photo of the robotics team posted on the school board before the last bell. Ms. Levy had promised the printer in the computer lab would work, and Tyson had the photo on his phone. But Tyson was slumped in front of a lab monitor, staring at a map.

"Someone knows where I am," he said. He pointed at the screen. "That star game. It's been following me. Look, it knows I was at the rink Tuesday, and at Ophelia's street on Saturday."

Isabelle leaned over his shoulder. The game had drawn a line through the whole week. She thought about her own phone, which her mother had made her check once, and a rule she half remembered. "Phones let you pick, app by app," she said. "An app can use your location always, only while you're using it, or never. Did you ever pick?"

Tyson scrolled through his settings. "I don't remember picking anything." He found the game in the list anyway. The screen said Always. He tapped it and a menu appeared with the three choices, exactly as she had said. He changed it to Never, then opened the game to see what would happen.

"It still plays," Tyson said. "It just asked for my location again and I said no." He sat back. He had wanted to delete the game entirely an hour ago, before Isabelle walked in. Now he changed his mind about that. "It's actually a good game. The star parliament level, where you have to stop the rebellious moons from leaving the orbit council. I don't want to lose my progress."

"The parliament is the fun part," Isabelle agreed. "Okay, but do the rest of your apps too." She pulled her chair beside his and they went down the list together. A weather app had Always as well, so they set it to While Using. The calculator said Never already. A photo app wanted Always, and Tyson hesitated, because he liked the map of pictures it made. "Your photos might get stored somewhere and strangers could see them if it's shared around," Isabelle said. "Ophelia posted a picture from her backyard once and some man she didn't know commented on it." Tyson set the photo app to While Using and shut the map off.

Then he said, "Your photo. For the board." He sent it to the lab printer, and it came out with a sound like it was trying to compress the whole picture into one thin page. The robotics team stared out from the paper, all four of them, standing in front of the shelf of parts.

Ms. Levy held the photo up to the light. "Nice. Tape's in my drawer." Isabelle took the tape and headed for the board in the hallway, and Tyson followed her, still holding his phone, reading out his list of apps as he walked. "One more," he said. "It says While Using. That one's fine, right?"

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the staff line for the note G.
story:
Mason had until Saturday to learn "Ode to Joy" on the piano, because Ms. Grant had appointed him to open the school talent show with it, and he had agreed before realizing he could not read a single note. He sat at the living room keyboard with the sheet music propped against a stack of cookbooks, poking at keys like someone testing a porus sponge to see which parts were actually solid.

Emy-Rose flopped onto the couch beside him with her own music, for trumpet, since she was performing too. "You've played that first measure eleven times," she said. "It hates you now."

"It doesn't hate me. I just can't find the notes on the page." Mason tapped the strange swirl at the start of every line. "And this thing keeps staring at me like it knows something."

Michel arrived carrying snacks, which he always did when someone was struggling, because he believed suffering went better with crackers. He leaned over the page. "My cousin calls that the G clef," he said. "I don't know why. Maybe it lost a bet."

Mason frowned. He traced the swirl with his finger, the way it curled around and looped through the five lines of the staff, and noticed something odd. The curl wrapped around the second line from the bottom and squeezed it like a hug. He counted up from the bottom line, his lips moving, then hunted along the keyboard until his finger landed on a key. He played it. Emy-Rose looked up from her trumpet.

"That's a G," she said. "How did you know that?"

"The clef told me. Look, it circles that line. G clef, G line." He tried the first measure again, and this time the notes came out in a shape that actually sounded like a song instead of a cat walking on the keys.

"Okay, that's weirdly brilliant," Michel said through a mouthful of cracker. "You appointed a swirl as your teacher."

Saturday morning, Mason waited behind the curtain with sweaty hands, watching Emy-Rose polish her trumpet and Michel give him a thumbs up. Ms. Grant whispered that the show was starting early, and that he would go on in one minute instead of two, which felt like being told a fire drill had moved up a day. He took a breath, sat at the big piano, and looked at the sheet music.

The twist hit him like a snowball. His pages were missing. The stage crew had set out the wrong music. But the first line still had that familiar swirl, curling around the second line up from the bottom, and Mason grinned at it like an old friend. "Found you," he whispered, put his fingers down, and began.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In much of Latin America, a cuadra is a city block, so directions like dos cuadras mean two blocks.
story:
"A bakery," Jonathan said, running down Abuela's front steps with his phrasebook flapping. "You really think I can find it all by myself?"

Abuela laughed from the doorway. "I have told you everything you need. Ask, listen, walk. And be back before noon, because we bake the bread together at twelve and the market will be crazy later." She said the last part in Spanish, fast, and Jonathan caught only "medio día," which he figured meant noon because "medio" was half and half of a day put you right at lunchtime. Malika had wanted to come along, but she was still upstairs helping Abuela wash the big clay pot, and she had made Jonathan promise to bring her back a pastry with pink sugar, which he intended to do even if it killed him.

His objective was simple: one loaf of bread and one pink pastry, back by noon. He practiced under his breath the whole way, "¿Dónde está la panadería?" until his mouth could say it without stumbling. At the corner, a man selling mangoes looked up, and Jonathan asked him. The man answered warmly, "Siga derecho, dos cuadras, a la derecha." Jonathan knew "derecho" was straight ahead, "derecha" was right, and "dos" was two, but "cuadras" was new. He decided it probably meant streets, since that was the only thing around to count. He walked straight, counting streets on his left. One street. Two streets. He kept going, because surely two streets meant a couple more after that, and he did not want to prolong the trip by asking again when he already had his answer.

At the fourth street he stopped. The houses here were small and dusty and there was no smell of bread. He turned around, and the thought arrived all at once, like the answer to a riddle he'd been chewing all morning. Maybe the man had counted the blocks between the streets, not the streets themselves. A cuadra wasn't a street, then, it was a block, a stretch of buildings between two corners. If he had turned right after two blocks, he would have turned at the second street, way back there. Jonathan spun around and speed-walked, half running, telling himself the whole way, "Cuadra means block, dos cuadras, two blocks." At the second street he turned right, and there it was, golden and glowing, with warm bread smell rolling out the door. Inside, the cashier raised her eyebrows at him. "¿Y tú qué quieres, joven?" Jonathan stood tall and answered in Spanish, "Un pan, por favor, y un dulce rosado." Then he checked the clock on the wall. Eleven forty. He grinned, paid, and tucked Malika's pastry carefully into his bag.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Astigmatism happens when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, which blurs vision at any distance.
story:
Xavier sat in the waiting room with the eye chart on the wall and the smell of lens cleaner in the air. His basketball game started at three, and it was already one thirty. At the far end of the room a poster showed a capital F, but the letter smeared sideways no matter how hard he squinted.

"Xavier," the optometrist called, and transported him down a dim hallway to a chair like something from a spaceship. Flipped lenses clicked in front of his face. "Which is better, one or two?"

"One." The letters sharpened, then fattened again. He tried an experiment of his own. He covered one eye, then the other, and the smear stayed in both, near and far. He held his hand out and read the small print on a box across the room. Blurred. He pulled the box close. Still blurred. "It's not a distance thing," he said. "Everything's fuzzy both ways."

The optometrist nodded. "That's astigmatism," he said, and sketched a quick oval on his notepad. "Your cornea, the clear window at the front of the eye, is slightly egg-shaped. It curves more in one direction than the other, so light doesn't focus cleanly. That blurs vision at any distance, near or far."

"So the ball at the far hoop and the playbook in my hands would both look smeared."

"Exactly."

The optometrist turned a dial, and the lens in front of Xavier snapped into a shape he could feel in the way the room suddenly settled. Every letter stood clean. "Better?"

"Way better. Can I get these today? My game's in an hour."

The optometrist checked a drawer, then held up a pair of wire-rimmed frames. "One variable. We have these in stock, or you order any frame you like and wait two weeks."

Xavier tried them on. The mirror showed a boy with sharp eyes and slightly crooked ears. He turned to the hallway clock and read the small red numbers without squinting.

"I'll take these."

At the game, Chace caught the ball on the wing and Xavier cut to the basket, open, because for the first time all season he could tell which defender was watching whom. The pass came straight and fast. He laid it in off the glass. On the bench afterward, grinning, Chace asked to try the glasses.

"Careful," Xavier said. "Squinting is contagious."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Quito, the capital of Ecuador, lies less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero.
story:
The atlas was heavier than David expected, and it fell open on the kitchen table with a thump that rattled his juice glass. He had told Ezekiel and Philippe that he would figure out the mystery city before either of them did, and he only had until dinner.

Ms. Nasser had left a folded note in his mailbox that afternoon, which was strange, because she lived three doors down and usually just waved. Inside, in her slanted handwriting, was a puzzle: "A capital city hides at nearly zero degrees south. Find it before your friends do, and the leftover empanadas are yours."

David stared at the note. Nearly zero degrees south. He knew latitude ran in lines across a map, and he knew the numbers told you how far north or south a place sat, but a capital city sitting at almost zero meant it had to hug the equator itself. He flipped to the spread of South America and dragged his finger along the printed line.

The phone buzzed. "I've got Greenland," Philippe's message read. "Nuuk. Sixty-four north. Take that."

David grinned and typed back, "Wrong hemisphere, genius." Then he set the phone face down, because Ezekiel would happily contribute three wrong guesses just to distract him, and David refused to be the antagonist of his own scavenger hunt. He needed to be impartial with himself, weighing each country fairly instead of grabbing the first one that looked likely.

Ecuador. The name almost said it, but he didn't trust almost. He found Quito on the map, then squinted at the tiny numbers along the map's edge, drawing his pencil straight up from the city until the pencil tip crossed a line. He checked it twice, holding his breath the second time.

Zero point two degrees south. Less than a quarter of a degree from the equator.

"Quito," he said out loud, alone in the kitchen. "The capital of Ecuador. Latitude almost zero."

He wrote the answer on the back of Ms. Nasser's note and jogged down the sidewalk before the sky turned any grayer. When she opened her door, he held it up, and she read it slowly, as if testing him.

"Quito," she said. "Well done. What's the latitude?"

"Almost zero," David said. "Less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator."

She stepped aside and pointed to a plate on the counter, still warm. "Fair is fair. Take two, and tell Ezekiel and Philippe they can contribute their guesses tomorrow, since they clearly contributed nothing tonight."

David was already reaching for an empanada when his phone buzzed one more time. "Brazilia?" Ezekiel had written.

"Wrong," David texted back, and hit send with his free hand.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Adding the tops and the bottoms separately gives a wrong answer: one half plus one third is five sixths, not two fifths.
story:
Dominic had been coming to the tutoring centre on Miller Street every Tuesday since September, and every Tuesday the fraction worksheet beat him. Today's problem sat near the top of the page: one half plus one third. He chewed his pencil, added the tops and the bottoms, and wrote two fifths. It looked right. It felt right.

Carly leaned over from the next desk, because Carly always finished first and collected a gold star from Ms. Clarke-Williams for every perfect sheet. She wanted ten stars before winter break, and she had eight. "Check that one," she said, tapping his paper. "Draw it. Shade half a chocolate bar, then a third of another one the same size."

He drew two rectangles and shaded them. Then, on a hunch, he drew a single bar and tried to shade two fifths of it. The shaded part was thinner than half the bar. He sat back. Somehow his answer was smaller than the half he had started with, even though he had added something to it. That could not be right.

Jamal slid his chair over, mumbling around a pretzel. "The bottoms have to match before you add. That's the trick." Dominic stared at his page, tried cutting both bars into six pieces, and wrote five sixths. This time the shaded amount was bigger than a half, bigger than a third, exactly what adding should do. Ms. Clarke-Williams, who ran the centre out of a storefront in the most affluent part of town, where the fee money went mostly to commerce in pencils and workbooks, walked past and put a check beside his answer. "Ten more minutes, everyone. Jamal, I'm going to allocate the last two pages to you, since you're fastest today." Jamal groaned, but he was already writing.

Carly raised her hand. "One more star?" she asked, holding up her finished sheet.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
Bennett had read the spelling list forty-two times, and the words still swam like minnows whenever he closed his eyes. The bee was Saturday, in the big room at the public library, and Oceanne had already promised to bring a banner that said BENNETT OR BUST, which was either support or a threat.

"You're doing it wrong," said his mother at dinner on Tuesday, flipping the list face down. "A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it."

"Who are those people?"

"Researchers. So tonight, I quiz you. No peeking."

Bennett groaned, but he let her hold the list like a card dealer. "Chrysanthemum."

He spelled it. He got it wrong. She made him try again, and then again, and something odd happened: the word stuck, like gum on a shoe. They did it every night, and by Friday he could spell words he'd only missed once, cold, no list, hands behind his back.

At the library on Saturday, Ms. MacLeod checked names at the door and would not permit anyone to bring snacks past the desk, which Bennett considered cruel and unusual. Anika was speller number three. He was speller number seven, right after a kid who cracked his knuckles like he was starting a lawnmower.

"Are you nervous?" Oceanne whispered, holding up her banner.

"No. I'm quizzed. There's a difference."

Round one: "garbage." Easy. Round two: "significant." Bennett asked for the definition, just to hear it, then spelled it clean. Round three knocked out Anika on "bureaucracy," which she took personally. Round four knocked out the knuckle-cracker on "rendezvous." Soon it was Bennett, one other kid, and a room so quiet he could hear the radiator valve hissing in the corner.

The other kid missed "rhinoceros," a crime against fourth graders everywhere. Ms. MacLeod adjusted her glasses and said, "Your word is valve."

Bennett almost laughed. His mother had drilled him on valve twice because he'd fumbled it Wednesday, twice more Thursday, once Friday. He could have spelled it in his sleep, standing on his head, in a hurricane.

"V-A-L-V-E. Valve."

"Correct." She paused. "For the win, one final word: chrysanthemum."

The word he'd missed three times at the dinner table, the word his mother had made him spell until he dreamed about it. Bennett grinned at the radiator, at Oceanne's wobbling banner, at Anika mouthing letters from the front row like a very unhelpful puppeteer.

"C-H-R-Y-S-A-N-T-H-E-M-U-M. Chrysanthemum."

Ms. MacLeod raised her hand. "We have a winner."

Oceanne shouted "OR BUST!" from the back, and his mother stood up holding the word list, then very slowly and ceremonially tore it in half.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: Every point on the graph of an equation is a solution to it; for y = 2x + 1, the point (3, 7) lies on the line because 2 times 3 plus 1 equals 7.
story:
Anais laid her pencil down like it was a dead thing. At the kitchen table, in front of her, sat a worksheet full of two-step equations and a coordinate grid with only one lonely dot on it. She wanted to finish before Friday, because Ms. Dlamini had promised the first three finishers could decorate the classroom bulletin board, and Anais had a plan involving glow-in-the-dark stars.

The doorbell rang, and Josue and Alizee came in carrying a bag of chips and their own crumpled worksheets. They had the same goal, which meant they were teammates and rivals at the same time. Josue flopped into a chair and studied her grid. "Your dot's in the wrong place," he announced. "No dot can be in the wrong place," Anais said. "It's a dot. It goes where it wants." "The dots on the line for y equals 2x plus 1," Alizee said, poking the paper. "That line signifies all the answers to the equation. If your dot's really on the line, the equation should work for it."

Anais narrowed her eyes. Her dot sat at (3, 7), where she had put it because it looked friendly over there. She wrote it out. Two times 3 was 6, and 6 plus 1 was 7. The equation worked. The point belonged on the line, every single number of it. She sat up so fast she knocked the chips onto the floor, and Alizee rescued them from under the table before the dog, who had the temperament of a hungry fungus, could get there first. "It's on the line," Anais said. "Because 2 times 3 plus 1 equals 7. So the dot is right."

"Then why does the line look like a snake that gave up?" Josue asked. He pointed at her three other points, which wandered all over the grid like lost socks. Anais tested each one. The point at (1, 5) failed, because 2 times 1 plus 1 was 3, not 5. She had been plotting the y before she'd solved for it, like eating dessert before finding out if there was dessert. She erased, recalculated, and plotted fresh dots that lined up as straight as soldiers. Then she connected them, and there was the line, clean and true.

They worked until the kitchen smelled like dinner and their mother told them to clear the table in ten minutes. Josue tried to claim the credit for the whole discovery. "Without my wrong comment about the dot," he said, "you'd never have tested it." "In vain, Josue," Anais said. "You tried to catch me being wrong, in vain." She held the finished worksheet up to the light like a treasure map, and the line caught the glow of the overhead lamp, straight from (0, 1) to the edge of the page.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: A five-paragraph essay has an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion.
story:
Lucas slid his essay across the table and watched Mr. Hussain's eyes move down the page. At the writing club meeting on Tuesdays, everyone brought a draft of a persuasive essay, and today's topic was one Lucas actually cared about: the school should fix the drinking fountains, because the water tasted like pennies.

"You've got a lot to say," Mr. Hussain said, tapping the paper.

"Too much?" Lucas asked.

"Count your paragraphs and see."

Lucas counted, pressing a finger to the page at each blank line. He got to the bottom and sat back. Seven. He counted again, in case his finger had skipped. Still seven. Across the table, Elle was counting hers too, mouthing the numbers.

"Why would the number matter, though?" Lucas wondered out loud. "Seven is more arguing. Seven is more convincing, isn't it?"

"Is it?" Elle said. "I stopped being convinced around paragraph five."

Malek leaned over from the next seat. "Mr. Hussain told me last week. A five-paragraph essay has an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion."

Lucas looked at his seven paragraphs and tried to sort them into those jobs. Introduction, that was easy, his first one. Conclusion, the last. That left five paragraphs in the middle for only three slots. So somewhere in there, he had written two paragraphs that were doing the same job twice without noticing. But which two? That was like figuring out which pipe in the wall was leaking; the plumbing was hidden, and he could only see the water.

He read each middle paragraph and gave it a secret label. Evidence about the taste. Evidence about the old filters. Another paragraph about the filters. A paragraph about how thirsty kids get after gym. A paragraph complaining that nobody listens to students. He circled the two filter paragraphs. They were twins. He hadn't seen it while he was writing, because the words were different even though the idea wasn't.

He crossed out one twin, moved the gym paragraph up, and slid the paper back to Mr. Hussain. "Five," he announced. "One, three, one."

Mr. Hussain raised an eyebrow. "And you were certain an hour ago that more paragraphs meant a stronger argument."

"I was immune to reason," Lucas admitted. "But I'm better now."

Elle laughed so hard she knocked over her pencil cup, and Malek picked up the pencils one by one and lined them up like fence posts.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: In email, BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy': people added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.
story:
Harrison sat at the kitchen computer with his mother's list of class email addresses beside him, printed in her careful handwriting. His birthday was on Saturday, and he wanted to invite the whole class to the park. He had typed the message three times already, because each version sounded wrong. "Hey everyone, come to my party," seemed too loud. "Dear classmates," sounded like a school assignment. He finally settled on "Hi! My birthday is Saturday and I'm having a party at Willow Park at two. I hope you can come."

The problem was the address bar. When he pasted the whole list into the To field, he could see every single address, all twenty-six of them, stretched across the screen. Haven had once told him that a kid in another class got teased because somebody forwarded a private message around. Harrison didn't fully understand how that worked, but he understood one thing: once you send something, you can't take it back.

He scrolled through the menu above the To field. There was a Cc line, and next to it, almost hidden, a link that said Add Bcc. He clicked it, and a new empty row appeared. The word Bcc didn't signify anything to him at first; it looked like three random letters. But the address book had a help page, and one line on it read: BCC stands for blind carbon copy. People added in the BCC field receive the message, but other recipients cannot see their addresses.

So he cut the whole list out of To, pasted it into the Bcc line, and typed his own address in To, all by itself. He stared at it for a while. It looked strange, like sending a letter to himself. He decided to test it before the real thing. He made a practice message, put his own address in To, put his friend Cole's address in Bcc, and wrote, "Test. Ignore this." Then he walked to Cole's house, two doors down, on a street that felt desolate in the late afternoon, all shut doors and empty driveways, and knocked.

Cole opened his laptop at the kitchen table and showed him the message. "It came to me," Cole said. "It says it's from you, and the To part just says your address. Mine isn't anywhere on it." Harrison leaned in and checked every line of the message, top to bottom. Cole was right. It was as if the email had arrived by magic, with no visible trail.

He walked home slowly, thinking it through. Public spaces, like the To field, showed everybody who was there. The Bcc line was a private space, invisible to the rest. It was like inviting people to a party by whispering to each of them separately, so nobody got a list of everybody else's names.

Back at the computer, he sent the real invitation. Within an hour, replies began to arrive, dropping one by one into his inbox. Cole wrote, "I'm coming, obviously." Haven wrote, "Will there be cake?" Harrison smiled and typed back, "Three kinds. It's a category all by itself." Then he opened his address book and started a new list, titled Party: People Coming, and typed the first name.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
story:
Juliette sat on the back porch steps at her grandmother's house, holding a plate of cake she was not eating, because the argument had started again. Finn, her cousin, insisted that Grandpa had let them ride the paddleboat alone two summers ago at the lake. Pierre-Olivier, her other cousin, said no, Grandpa had never let them, that they had snuck out and Grandpa had only pretended not to notice so nobody would get in trouble. They had been arguing about it since the potato salad.

"You weren't even paying attention," Finn said, jabbing his fork toward Pierre-Olivier. "I remember the whole thing. He waved us off from the dock."

"He waved at the Lochners' boat," Pierre-Olivier said. "I asked him about it last Christmas and he laughed."

Juliette had been there too, but when she closed her eyes and went back to the lake, she found she could see it both ways. In one version, Grandpa stood at the dock and waved them out, sun on the water. In the other, the dock was empty and the screen door had banged behind them. The two memories felt exactly the same, equally real, and that was the strange part.

"I'm doing a diagnosis," she announced, which made both boys stop chewing. "Of the argument. Not of you." She stood up. The gradual dusk was settling over the yard, and Aunt Renée was trying to supervise six kids and a grill at once from a lawn chair, which was not going well. Juliette had learned the word from her mother, who used it whenever two people were certain about opposite things and could not both be right. "There's a name for it," her mother had said once, drying dishes. "When you're sure you see the world the way it really is, so anyone who disagrees must be uniformed or biased. That's called naive realism." Juliette had looked it up and copied it into her notebook, and now she took the notebook out of her back pocket.

She read the line out loud on the porch. Finn frowned. Pierre-Olivier frowned harder, because the line meant he might be the biased one, and Juliette could see him realizing it, which was almost funny.

"Wait," Finn said slowly. "So if I think you're wrong and you think I'm wrong, and we're both totally sure?"

"Then you're both doing it," Juliette said. "Both."

Pierre-Olivier set down his plate. "Okay," he said. "Test it. We ask Grandpa. Right now. And whoever's wrong has to carry the diagnosis notebook home in their teeth."

"Deal," said Finn, already halfway across the yard, and Juliette followed, notebook in hand, toward the porch swing where Grandpa sat shelling peanuts in the last of the light.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team, the first time any professional athlete was honored that way.
story:
Grandpa's living room smelled like popcorn and old leather, and every seat was taken. Alexandra squeezed onto the rug between her friends Veronika and Mika, while the TV showed the pregame show and the adults argued about whether Grandpa's new television had been worth the price.
