"Worth it, my foot," Grandpa muttered from his armchair. "The tariff on imported electronics nearly doubled what I paid." Alexandra filed that away to ask about later, because right now something on the screen had caught her eye.

"Wait," Mika said, leaning forward. "Look at all the jersey numbers. Every single player has a different one. Is that a rule? Like, does nobody ever share a number?" Alexandra studied the screen, counting. "They can share, I think, but not on the same team." Then another question formed, the kind she couldn't shake. "But here's the weird thing. Have you ever seen a player wearing 42? Any team, any game?" Veronika frowned. "No. But I've never really looked."

So they looked. Alexandra grabbed the stack of brittle old sports magazines from under the coffee table, careful not to crack the yellowed pages, and the three of them hunted through every team photo. Numbers everywhere: 7, 23, 51, 34. Never 42. "It's like the number got erased," Veronika whispered. Alexandra felt that pleasant itch she got when a pattern was hiding something. Maybe nobody wanted it? Maybe it was bad luck? She flipped to the front of the oldest magazine, and there it was, in a headline from 1997: every Major League Baseball team had retired number 42, for Jackie Robinson. She read further, mouth open. It was the first time any professional athlete had ever been honored that way, by every team at once.

"That's why," she said, holding up the page. "Nobody's allowed to wear 42. They retired it everywhere, all the way back in 1997." Grandpa craned his neck from his chair. "So you found my old magazine. Your great-grandmother saved that one." Mika grinned. "So if I ever get drafted, I can't pick 42 for my walk-up song number either?" "You could embarrass yourself trying," Alexandra said, and Veronika laughed so hard she knocked over the popcorn bowl.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Each year the Nile flooded Egypt in late summer, fed by heavy summer rains in the highlands of Ethiopia far to the south.
story:
Laurence spread her notes across the library table and glared at them, as if glaring had ever made homework go faster. Mr. Perera had assigned one page on the pyramids, and his criterion was strict: the answer had to explain why, not just what. "The Nile flooded every year and made the soil rich, so farmers could grow extra grain to feed the workers," she read aloud. "Whoa. Hold on."

Elliana looked up from her book. "You said whoa. That's a big word for a Tuesday."

"Look at this map." Laurence jabbed a finger at Egypt. "Desert here, desert there, basically desert everywhere. And yet the Nile flooded every single year. Where does a river in a desert get that much water? It doesn't rain there. It barely rains at all."

Lucian leaned over, chewing his pencil like it owed him money. "Maybe the river just refills itself. Magic river."

"Rivers don't do magic." Laurence flipped pages, faster now, hunting. Then she remembered last summer, when her family drove through a rainstorm so fierce that the dry creek near her grandmother's house turned into a brown river in an afternoon, and stayed that way for days even though the sun came out. Things downstream could change because of weather somewhere else. Her pencil started moving before she'd finished the thought. She traced the Nile south with her finger, out of Egypt, past the deserts, up into the highlands far to the south. Ethiopia. The caption under the map made her want to shout in a library, which was against every rule: heavy summer rains in the Ethiopian highlands fed the river, so Egypt's flood arrived in late summer.

"So it rains a whole country away," she said, "and Egypt gets flooded. Egypt gets somebody else's weather, delivered by river."

"Like mail," said Lucian. "Wet mail."

Laurence wrote the last line of her report and held it up. "Feasible. Factual. One full page." She paused. "If I read it out loud tomorrow and it works, you have to cease calling it the Magic River."

"Deal," said Elliana, and shook her hand over the map of Ethiopia.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Since Canada stopped distributing pennies in 2013, cash totals there are rounded to the nearest five cents, while card payments are still charged to the exact cent.
story:
Luca stood at the bus stop with a five-dollar bill folded in his pocket and his mother's short list running through his head: walk to the corner store, buy one carton of milk, count the change before leaving. The milk cost three dollars and two cents, according to the sticker he'd memorized yesterday. He had practiced the math at the kitchen table. Five dollars minus three dollars and two cents meant one dollar and ninety-eight cents coming back.

Inside the store, the cashier rang up the milk and Luca handed over his five. He watched the register screen, ready to count. The cashier gave him two dollars exactly. Luca stared at the coins in his palm. "Wait," he said. "The milk is three oh two. Shouldn't I get one ninety-eight?"

The cashier tapped the screen. "Not when you pay cash. Since we stopped getting pennies in Canada in 2013, cash totals get rounded to the nearest five cents. Three oh two rounds down to three dollars even." She shrugged. "Cards still get charged to the exact cent, though. Three oh two on a card, three dollars in cash."

Luca stepped aside so the man behind him could pay. He lined up his coins on the counter's edge and counted them twice, testing the idea. Two dollars back meant the store had charged exactly three dollars. He thought of a pattern: any price ending in one or two cents would round down, and a price ending in three or four would have to round up. He would check that next time with something that cost, say, one ninety-three.

Outside, he found Celina waiting at the bus stop with her backpack dragging off one shoulder. "Did you get sent alone?" she asked. "My mom still won't let me."

"I did, and I already found a trick," Luca said. He held up the milk carton like a trophy and gave the receipt a small flourish. "Prices ending in two are your friend. Pay cash, and it rounds down."

Celina squinted at the receipt. "That doesn't seem fair to people paying by card."

"Maybe not," Luca admitted. "The rounding doesn't care what you think. It's completely impartial." He dropped the coins into his pocket one at a time, listening to them clink. "Tomorrow I'm buying bread. One ninety-eight. My technique is to bring exactly two dollars."

Celina laughed. "That's just... paying."

"Try it," Luca said, and started down the sidewalk with the milk swinging in his hand.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Repeating an experiment several times helps show whether a result is real or just happened by chance.
story:
Bruno set the plywood ramp across two stable stacks of paint cans, and his green car, the one with the camouflage stickers, shot down and crossed the chalk line a whole hand ahead of Kayla's blue one. "Fastest car forever," Bruno announced. "Nobody can beat it. Ever."

Kayla picked up the blue car and turned it over in her hands. She had a guess forming, something she couldn't see but could almost feel: her car wasn't slower, the wheels were just sticky, and if she cleaned them, the result would flip. That was her whole plan, a testable guess, and she meant to test it. "One race doesn't prove anything," she said. "You have to run it a bunch of times. Repeating an experiment shows whether a result is real or whether it just happened by chance." Bruno folded his arms. He wanted his title, and he wanted it announced to the whole grade by Monday.

She wiped each wheel with a rag and a drop of oil from her dad's workbench. Then they raced again. Green won. They raced three more times, and blue won twice, green once. Kayla frowned at the ramp itself. The paint cans on the right side had shifted, and that side of the ramp sagged like a tired shoulder. Whichever lane was downhill-leaning won, no matter which car rode it.

"Swap lanes," she said. They did, and the camouflage car lost three races in a row in the crooked lane. Bruno groaned, but Kayla was already wedging a folded scrap of cardboard under the low side until the ramp sat stable. Then they ran five clean races, trading lanes each time. Blue won three, green won two.

"So mine's faster, but only a little," Kayla said. "And yours isn't slow, it's just not a forever champion." Bruno studied his car for a long moment. "Okay," he said slowly, "then I want a rematch with better wheels. My dad's got sandpaper in our garage." He held out his hand for the rag and the oil.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: U.S. sleep experts recommend 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
story:
Joseph taped the tryout notice to his bedroom door and counted backward. Basketball tryouts started at eight in the morning on Saturday, and he would need to wake at seven to eat and stretch. That gave him a puzzle he could actually solve: how early did he have to go to bed?

He messaged Brennan, whose older sister had printed a chart from a sleep clinic for her health class. Brennan snapped a photo of it and sent it over. Joseph read it twice. Children aged six to twelve needed nine to twelve hours of sleep a night, while teenagers needed only eight to ten. He was ten, so nine hours meant lights out at ten o'clock. He could still squeeze in one game with Pascal online first, he decided, and still generate a solid ten hours of rest.

Pascal kept winning match after match. "One more," Pascal typed at ten-fifteen. Then ten-forty. Joseph finally shut the screen at eleven, which still left him eight hours if he fell asleep instantly. He did not. The streetlight flickered on his ceiling, and the house was so tranquil that he could hear the refrigerator humming downstairs. When the alarm went off, his legs felt like they belonged to someone else.

At breakfast he watched his little brother bounce a tennis ball off the floor and felt something twist in his mood. Brennan had slept nine and a half hours. Joseph had slept maybe six. His ankles were stiff, and when he touched the cord of tendon above his heel, it felt tight as a shoelace pulled too hard. He tried a slow jog to the mailbox to test it, then quick feet on the porch steps. Sluggish, but holding.

Monday afternoon, Joseph ran home from the bus stop and burst through the kitchen door. His mom looked up from the sink, a dish towel in her hand.

"Second string," Joseph panted, grinning. "But Coach says I move up if I keep showing up. And Brennan made first." He dropped his backpack on a chair. "New rule, and it starts tonight. Ten o'clock, lights out, no exceptions."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
story:
Austin's hockey team had lost every away game that season, seven in a row, but they had won all three games at their own rink. He sat on the bench after practice, spinning a puck on its edge, and started writing the scores in the frost on the glass with his glove. Loss, loss, loss, loss, loss, loss, loss. Then, in a column beside it: win, win, win.

"It's not random," he told Memphis, who was unlacing his skates two seats down. "Random would be mixed up. This is a pattern. We stink everywhere except here."

Memphis looked at the frost columns. "Maybe our rink is lucky."

"Lucky isn't a thing," Austin said. "There has to be a reason."

That night he looked it up on the library computer, clicking through three articles before he found it. Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average. Some people called it home advantage. He read the sentence twice, then wrote it on his wrist tape.

At the next practice, Mr. Romano, who ran the snack bar and had played junior hockey for eleven years, watched Austin tape his stick. "What's written there?"

"Home advantage," Austin said. "It means home teams win more than half their games on average. Across lots of sports."

Mr. Romano snorted. "So you're saying we should never leave the building."

"That's the plan," Austin said. "Also, I have a real plan."

The plan was this. Since the rink felt different to visiting teams, Austin decided the away games must feel different in a way he could mimic. He noticed that at home the team always arrived early, warmed up slowly, and skated their familiar laps before the crowd came in. On the road they tumbled off the bus ten minutes before the whistle. So he begged the coach to leave an hour earlier for the Saturday game in Coralie's town, where Coralie had promised to bring a bunch of classmates to cheer.

The coach agreed to try it once. The team arrived early, skated slow laps, and did their exact home warmup, even lining up for passes in the same order. Coralie's group banged the glass behind their bench, which was against away protocol but not against the rules. Austin scored on a rebound in the second period, and they won by one.

On the bus home, Memphis leaned over the seat. "So did we beat home advantage or copy it?"

Austin peeled the tape off his wrist and stuck it to the window. "We borrowed it."

The puck from the win was still in his glove, cold against his palm.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
Justin sat at the kitchen table with a magnifying glass in one hand and a crumbly gray rock in the other. For his science project he had to photograph lichen, the patchy stuff that grew on stones and old fences, and he had found the perfect sample on Mr. Haddad's garden wall next door. His mother had said he could invite friends over on Saturday to help him collect more, but only if they planned it today, because she needed to accompany them on the walk to the creek and wanted to know numbers in advance.

He opened the group chat. Zayne and Andy were both listed as online. Justin typed, "want to come to the creek Saturday to look at rocks?" and waited. Nothing. He could hear his mother washing dishes, smell the lemon soap, hear the squeak of the sponge going round and round. The chat stayed silent. Zayne and Andy usually answered fast, especially when snacks were involved, so Justin figured his message had gotten buried under the fifty other messages about weekend plans.

He tried again, typing bigger to get noticed: "WHERE ARE YOU GUYS, CREEK SATURDAY?" He hit send. This time the answer came at once, three dots, then Andy's reply: "why are you yelling?" Justin stared at the screen. Yelling? He had barely whispered. Then Zayne wrote, "you typed in all caps, it looks like shouting." Justin looked at his message again. The big letters did seem loud, the way a teacher looked just before raising her voice. He typed back, "sorry, didn't know caps meant shouting, I just wanted you to see it."

"we see it," Zayne wrote. "creek sounds great. is there food." Justin laughed out loud, loud enough that his mother turned around with the sponge still in her hand. He typed an explicit answer so nothing could be misunderstood: "Sandwiches, chips, lemonade, ten o'clock Saturday, my house." Both friends replied with a single thumbs up.

Justin set the phone down and picked up the magnifying glass again, tilting it until the lichen bloomed into a tiny green forest on the gray stone. His mother dried her hands and said, "I'll buy extra lemonade, then." Justin grinned and wrote one last message in careful lowercase: "bring boots, it might be muddy."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
Jaxson stood outside the Buddhist temple with his shoes already off, which was rule number one, and his gift bag sweating in his hand, which was rule number two: you never visited Kenji's grandmother empty-handed. Camila had prescribed exactly this kind of wrapped soap set, "fancy, but not too fancy," and he'd spent twenty minutes at the shop deciding.

Inside, the temple smelled like incense and old wood. A crack ran up one stone pillar, and Kenji's grandfather noticed Jaxson staring at it. "Erosion," the old man said in careful English, patting the stone like a tired animal. "Water wins, slowly." Jaxson nodded, then remembered what Kenji had taught him last week: nodding wasn't the greeting here, bowing was. And the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it showed.

The problem was the math of it. Kenji's grandfather had just bowed about fifteen degrees, quick and light, like flicking water off his fingers. Kenji's grandmother had bowed lower and slower, holding it while Jaxson panicked about his shoes. So how deep was he supposed to go back? He'd tested a hypothetical version in his bedroom mirror until his little brother asked if he was having stomach trouble. Now the real grandfather stood in front of him, waiting.

Jaxson reasoned it out: grandfather gave a light bow, so a giant floor-scraping bow back would be weird, like shouting THANK YOU at someone who'd whispered hi. He matched the older man's depth and held it a beat longer, because you could never go wrong adding respect.

The grandfather's eyes crinkled. "Good bow," he said, and stuck out his hand for a handshake, which made Jaxson laugh so hard he had to bow again.

Later, at the long table in the temple's dining hall, Jaxson slurped his noodles on purpose, loud and proud, because Kenji had sworn it was a compliment here. His mother, visiting next month, was going to need a whole list.

"More tea?" asked Kenji's grandmother, already pouring.

"Yes, please," Jaxson said, and bowed from his chair, just to see her smile.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: In a chemical change the total mass stays the same; burning wood only seems to lose mass because the gases it makes escape into the air.
story:
The science lab smelled like vinegar and burnt matches, which Isabella decided was the smell of learning. Ms. Diallo had set out three stations: a melting ice cube, a rusty nail in a jar, and a candle on a digital scale. The assignment sheet said to label each one a physical change or a chemical change, but the candle station had a second question at the bottom, and that question was going to ruin Isabella's afternoon: "Where did the missing mass go?"

"Sixty-two grams before," Gurshaan read off the sticky note beside the candle. "Now it says fifty-nine."

"That's three grams gone," Isabella said. "Stuff can't just evaporate into nothing." She held the scale's tray up to the light as if the missing grams might be hiding underneath it.

Rylee, who had finished the melting ice station, wandered over with her notebook. "Maybe the scale is broken," she offered. Isabella shook her head, because the rusty nail had weighed exactly the same as the day before, jar and all, and the same scale had measured that just fine. So the scale worked, the nail followed the rule she'd half-remembered from the textbook, and the candle was breaking it anyway.

Then she thought about the smoke. It curled up from the wick in a thin gray ribbon and vanished near the ceiling. It was going somewhere. It had to be going somewhere with mass attached. She turned to Rylee. "The missing mass went into the air. Burning the candle made gases, and they escaped. So the mass didn't disappear, we just can't see where it went."

Rylee looked at her with frank skepticism. "You're telling me smoke weighs three grams?"

"We could test it," Isabella said, and she wrote a quick note to Ms. Diallo on a scrap of paper, since the teacher was across the room with the ice cube group: "Can we burn the candle under something that catches the smoke? Signed, Isabella." Ms. Diallo read it, smiled, and brought over a large glass jar with a lid.

They set the candle inside the jar on the scale, lit it, and sealed the lid. The flame burned tranquil and steady behind the glass while the three of them watched the numbers. When the flame finally shrank and went out, Isabella leaned close to the display.

"Sixty-two grams," she said. "Minus the tiny bit that melted onto the glass, but still. It's all still in there."

Gurshaan pressed his finger against the warm jar. "The smoke's stuck to the inside. Look, it's all foggy up at the top."

"Write it down before we forget," Rylee said, sliding the notebook across the counter to her.

Jeremy flopped onto the couch with the laptop and typed "jaguar" into the search bar. His school project was due Friday, and Mr. Mansour had asked for ten real facts about the animal, not one sentence and a poster covered in glitter.

The first page of results was all car dealerships. "Test drive the 2025 jaguar!" "Jaguar specials, this week only!" One result had a tiny grey word beside it that said "Ad," which was how Jeremy noticed that half the page was trying to sell him something. He scrolled and scrolled until his patience began to erode like a sandcastle at high tide. Somewhere under all those shiny cars, there had to be an actual cat.

His phone buzzed. It was a message from Lea-Maude.

Lea-Maude: My mom says jaguars can sense fish with their paws?? Is that true or did she make it up because she wants me to stop asking about sharks? Also bring the good markers tomorrow.

Jeremy grinned and typed back that he would investigate, though he privately suspected her mom just liked inventing animal facts. He tried "jaguar facts." Cars again. He tried "jaguar animal." Better, but a page about jaguar car floor mats still snuck in, wearing a headline that looked sinister with all its capital letters and too many exclamation points.

He stared at the keyboard. The cars kept showing up because the word jaguar meant both things. What if he could tell the search engine which one to throw away? On a wild guess, he typed: jaguar -car. He pressed enter, holding his breath like the laptop might need a moment to think.

The dealerships vanished. Every result on the page was spots, whiskers, and jungle. Jeremy pumped both fists in the air, nearly knocking over a lamp.

"Big cats?" his dad asked from the doorway.

"Big cats," Jeremy said. He copied the search into his notes: jaguar -car. A minus sign right before a word, no space after it, and the search dropped that word like a hot rock.

He found the paw fact, too. Some scientists think a jaguar can detect ripples, almost like its paw works as a sensor for movement in the water, which helps it fish at night. Lea-Maude's mom had been right, which Jeremy decided not to tell her, because Lea-Maude enjoyed being right far too much already.

His phone buzzed again.

Lea-Maude: Did you find out about the paws or are you just looking at funny cat videos? Be honest.

Jeremy typed back: "Would I lie to a girl with seventeen good markers?"

He hit send, then turned the laptop so the screen faced the window, where the evening light caught the jaguar's golden eyes staring out from the dark green jungle.
